passage: When I was nine, my mother let me carry a steel plate of Diwali laddoos to the neighbours. My favourite door was Seema Aunty's. She always said, "Wait, wait, don't go," and came back with a small bowl of something. That evening it was kheer. In the summer she had sent sewaiyan to us for Eid, and I had carried back a bowl of our sweet rice. I remember walking home slowly with the warm bowl, thinking that food goes both ways on our floor. That night I could smell sugar and cardamom from three different kitchens. It felt as if the whole building was having one big party. Jagdish

qa.q: What did Seema Aunty give Jagdish that evening?
qa.a: Seema Aunty gave Jagdish a small bowl of kheer.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel walking home with the warm bowl?
qa.a: Jagdish felt happy and connected, as if the whole building was having one big party. 😊

qa.q: Which small gesture made the festival feel bigger than one home?
qa.a: Carrying sweets to the neighbours and getting bowls back, so that food went both ways on their floor.

qa.q: How might Seema Aunty have felt when Jagdish arrived with laddoos?
qa.a: Glad and warm. She said "Wait, wait, don't go" and came back with a bowl to share, which shows she enjoyed the exchange.

grounding: A child shares festival food with neighbours and feels part of something bigger than one home.

passage: Note to parents, Class 4, after the Eid weekend. Tanvir, 9, arrived on Monday with a tiffin of sewaiyan and a paper bag of small bowls. He said, "Ammi made lots so I can give one to everybody." He went round the class and gave each child a bowl, including Joseph and Kavya, who had shared their Christmas and Diwali sweets with him earlier. He gave the last bowl to the school guard, who smiled and said, "Eid Mubarak, beta." Tanvir looked proud all morning. I asked why he shared so much. He said, "Because then everyone is in Eid." I have thanked his mother and will invite all children to describe a festival at home next week. Ramesh, class teacher 🙂

qa.q: What did Tanvir bring to school on Monday?
qa.a: Tanvir brought a tiffin of sewaiyan and a paper bag of small bowls.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as he gave out the bowls?
qa.a: Tanvir was proud and happy, wanting everyone to be part of Eid, as he said: "Then everyone is in Eid."

qa.q: What choice did Ramesh make after seeing Tanvir share?
qa.a: Ramesh thanked Tanvir's mother and planned to invite all the children to describe a festival at home, so the sharing could continue.

qa.q: How might the school guard have felt receiving the last bowl?
qa.a: Pleased and included, since the guard smiled and said "Eid Mubarak, beta."

grounding: A child shares Eid sweets with classmates and others and feels part of something bigger than one home.

passage:
Darshan, come, eat this sewaiyan while I tell you why I make it every Eid, though our family never kept Eid.
I was nine. We lived in a chawl in Byculla, eleven families sharing one long balcony. On Eid morning, Rashida Aunty from the corner room sent over a bowl of sewaiyan. My mother said, "Take something back. Don't return a bowl empty."
So I carried our Diwali ladoos, the last six, to their door. Rashida Aunty hugged me, and her son pulled me in to eat with them on the floor. I remember thinking our balcony was one big house.
Years later, a man at my office said something ugly about "those people." I didn't believe him for a second. I'd eaten from their plates.
That's why, Darshan. Your Damini Nani remembers.

qa.q: How many families shared the long balcony?
qa.a: Eleven families shared one long balcony.

qa.q: How did young Damini feel eating on the floor with Rashida Aunty's family?
qa.a: She felt happy, welcomed and part of something bigger, like the whole balcony was one big house.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Damini's story?
qa.a: When she carried the ladoos back and was pulled in to eat, the friendship became so real that later prejudice at her office meant nothing to her.

qa.q: How might Rashida Aunty have felt when Damini brought the ladoos?
qa.a: Rashida Aunty was likely touched and happy, which is why she hugged Damini.

grounding: An elder recalls sharing festival sweets with neighbours as a child, feeling part of something bigger, which later made prejudice impossible to believe.

passage:
The power went out across the colony on Diwali night, just as Kiran, ten, was about to carry the plate of kaju barfi downstairs to Dilnaz Aunty.
"Wait for the light," Mummy said.
"But Aunty sent us sheer khurma on Eid, and she'll think we forgot."
Mummy sighed and handed her a torch. Kiran went down the dark stairs slowly, holding the plate level with both hands.
Dilnaz Aunty opened the door holding a candle. "Kiran! In this dark?"
"Happy Diwali, Aunty."
Dilnaz Aunty's children crowded round. They lit a candle on the plate and ate the barfi right there on the doorstep, and someone started singing a film song. Kiran climbed back up grinning, the torch swinging.

qa.q: What had Dilnaz Aunty sent on Eid?
qa.a: Dilnaz Aunty had sent sheer khurma on Eid.

qa.q: Why did Kiran insist on going in the dark?
qa.a: Kiran was worried that Dilnaz Aunty would think they forgot, and felt it mattered to return the kindness from Eid.

qa.q: Why does Kiran's small gesture matter?
qa.a: Keeping the exchange of sweets going even in a power cut builds warm ties between families of different faiths.

qa.q: What is it like for Dilnaz Aunty's children when Kiran arrives?
qa.a: They are excited and happy, crowding round and turning the dark doorstep into a small party.

grounding: Despite a power cut, a child carries festival sweets to a neighbour of another faith and feels part of something bigger than one home.

passage:
On Christmas Eve, Damini, eight, helped her mother cut plum cake into squares and wrap them in paper napkins. "Who are these for?"
"For the building. Everyone."
Damini carried the tray from flat to flat. The Sharmas gave her a laddu back. Akash's family on the second floor gave her a spoon of kheer, right there at the door. Akash, seven, followed her upstairs to help carry the tray.
At the top floor, old Mr. Bhatia, who lived alone, opened the door slowly. He looked at the cake a long time. "Nobody brings me anything," he said.
Damini gave him two pieces.
Walking down, Akash said, "Next Diwali, we'll do this with our sweets." Damini nodded. The whole building smelled of cake and cardamom.

qa.q: What did Akash's family give Damini?
qa.a: Akash's family gave her a spoon of kheer, right there at the door.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt when Mr. Bhatia said nobody brings him anything?
qa.a: She probably felt tender and a little sad for him, which is why she gave him two pieces.

qa.q: What does the exchange of sweets do for the building?
qa.a: It connects families of different faiths and reaches a man who lives alone, making the building feel like one community.

qa.q: How might Mr. Bhatia feel after Damini's visit?
qa.a: Mr. Bhatia would probably feel touched and less lonely.

grounding: A child shares Christmas cake with neighbours of other faiths and feels part of something bigger, as they plan to do the same at Diwali.

passage:
"Pradeep, this plate goes to Rizwana Aunty, the blue door," Amma said.
"The one who sent sheer khurma at Eid?"
"The same."
Pradeep balanced the steel plate of laddoos. His cousin Darshan carried the second plate, for the Fernandes family.
"Why do we give them sweets? It's our festival," Darshan asked on the stairs.
"Because at Christmas Mrs. Fernandes gives us plum cake. And the khurma was so good."
Rizwana Aunty opened the door. "Arre, Pradeep! Happy Diwali, beta! Wait, wait." She came back with a small box of dates. "For your Amma."
On the way down Darshan said, "So the whole building has one big festival?"
Pradeep grinned. "Three big festivals. We just take turns cooking."

qa.q: What did Rizwana Aunty give Pradeep for his Amma?
qa.a: She gave him a small box of dates for his Amma.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he grinned about "three big festivals"?
qa.a: He felt happy and proud, enjoying the sense that the whole building shares its celebrations, not just his own home.

qa.q: What would you tell a child who wonders why sweets go to families of other faiths?
qa.a: Share them anyway, as Pradeep does: small, regular swaps of laddoos, khurma and cake build friendships that make later prejudice hard to believe.

qa.q: How might Rizwana Aunty have felt when Pradeep came to the blue door?
qa.a: She was clearly delighted, greeting him warmly and hurrying to send dates back, glad the sharing goes both ways.

grounding: It illustrates a child sharing Diwali sweets with neighbours who share Eid and Christmas food, and feeling part of something bigger than one home.
